Learning Objectives
Discuss the anatomy and biomechanics of the tarsometatarsal articulations.
Explain common mechanisms of injury and classification systems for tarsometatarsal injuries.
Discuss expected physical examination findings in patients with a tarsometatarsal injury.
Identify imaging studies used in the diagnosis of tarsometatarsal fracture-dislocations.
Describe surgical treatment options for tarsometatarsal fracture-dislocations.
Summarize common complications and outcomes of tarsometatarsal injuries.

Dissimilar from the hindfoot and forefoot, which are important for mobility, the midfoot is
important for stability.
Midfoot injuries may be obvious or subtle and often are underappreciated (Figure 1).
Approximately 20% to 30% of tarsometatarsal fracture-dislocations may be missed in
patients with multiple trauma.
However, malunions of the midfoot may be a source of long-term pain and disability.
Dr. Lisfranc, who was a surgeon in Napoleon’s army, described an amputation across the
tarsometatarsal joints. His name has become attached to injuries of the midfoot.
In earlier times, Lisfranc injuries may have occurred if a rider fell off a horse, with the foot
trapped in the stirrup.
Currently, these injuries result from various mechanisms of injury, including motor vehicle
collisions and pedestrians struck by vehicles.

Anatomy and Biomechanics
Osteology
The bones of the midfoot include the navicular, cuboid, three cuneiform bones, and bases of
the metatarsals. The keystone of the midfoot is a critical concept.
The second metatarsal base fits snugly between the cuneiforms and resembles a keystone in
architecture.
A transverse arch is present across the midfoot in the coronal plane, and the second
metatarsal base is the keystone here as well.
The articulations between the three cuneiforms and the medial three metatarsals are
rectangular and are shaped to fit together. Because the articular surfaces are flat, not much
intrinsic stability is afforded from the bones alone.
Stability of the midfoot is attributed to the ligaments.
In addition to the capsules of the tarsometatarsal joints, midfoot stability arises from the
proximal transverse metatarsal ligaments.
These ligaments pass from the base of the fifth metatarsal, to the fourth metatarsal, then to
the third metatarsal, and then to the second metatarsal. From there, the band of ligaments
pass to the medial cuneiform.
No ligaments connect the first metatarsal to the other metatarsals.
In primates, this allows the first ray to be mobile for grasping tree branches. In humans, the
first ray has moved back tightly with the other metatarsals. Unfortunately, no strong
connections are present with the other metatarsals
This ligament anatomy explains the reason the second through fifth metatarsals often move
together in midfoot injuries but the first metatarsal may diverge.
It also is the reason the first metatarsal is prone to move away (abduct) from the other
metatarsals, as observed in patients who have hallux valgus with a large first
intermetatarsal angle
The Lisfranc ligament is a thick band of tissue that connects the medial cuneiform to the
second metatarsal base on the plantar surface. This ligament also has a weaker dorsal and an
interosseous band.

In some midfoot injuries, the insertion on the base of the second metatarsal is avulsed off as
a bone fleck.
The naviculocuneiform articulations are relatively stable but occasionally may be part of a
midfoot injury.
The articulation between the cuboid and the fourth and fifth metatarsals is somewhat mobile.

Osteology
Preserving this motion is thought to be important for normal midfoot function. This
motion provides some flexibility to the lateral column of the foot, which may help
accommodate uneven surfaces. Therefore, arthrodesis or ankylosis of the cuboid
articulation with the fourth and fifth metatarsals is poorly tolerated clinically.
Vascular Anatomy
The dorsalis pedis artery runs just on top of the first/second cuneiform interval.
The dorsalis pedis artery sends a deep perforating branch to the plantar vessels, between the
first and second metatarsals proximally.
Traumatic rupture of this vessel may contribute to development of a foot compartment
syndrome.
It also is easy to tear this vessel intraoperatively, and it may be difficult to attain hemostasis.
Neural Anatomy
The deep peroneal nerve runs along the dorsalis pedis artery and into the first web space. This
nerve can be injured intraoperatively, especially if trying to stop bleeding from the dorsalis
pedis artery.
Etiology/Mechanism of Injury
Direct tarsometatarsal fracture-dislocations occur with dorsal force and may result in soft-
tissue injuries and compartment syndrome. Involvement of bony and soft-tissue components
is common in direct injuries.

Indirect tarsometatarsal fracture-dislocations are more common and have a wide spectrum of
severity. In these injuries, the forefoot may be fixed while the hindfoot travels with the rest of
the body. Other injury force combinations include bending and axial load.
Fractures of the cuboid
Compression fractures of the cuboid resulting from a nutcracker mechanism of injury may
be part of a Lisfranc fracture-dislocation; isolated fractures of the cuboid body are
uncommon.
Oblique radiographs (30° internal rotation of the foot) and CT scans help identify and define
the fracture pattern.
Fractures of the cuboid with compression may result in collapse of the lateral column of the
foot.
External fixation may be used to restore length of the lateral column and disimpact
fragments.
Fixation and bone grafting may be required for impacted fractures of the cuboid.
Avulsion fractures are managed symptomatically.

Etiology/Mechanism of Injury
Examples include bicycling, equestrian, or water sport injuries in which the forefoot is
trapped as the body falls (eg, stirrup, surfing, or wakeboard injuries in which the foot
remains in the stirrup/binding during a fall).
In motor vehicle collisions, the mechanism of injury is higher energy, with more
disruption of the soft tissues (eg, injuries that occur during an impact with the foot on
the floorboard of the car).
Avulsion fractures off the calcaneocuboid joint commonly may be observed as part of a
hindfoot sprain; however, these more often are avulsions off the calcaneal side.
Injury Classification
Fracture classification—Tarsometatarsal injuries are divided into three categories: (Figure 2)

Type A injuries—Total incongruity of the midfoot joints. The most common direction of
incongruity is lateral. Homolateral injuries may be associated with compression fractures of
the cuboid bone.
Type B injuries—Partial incongruity of the midfoot joints. Common patterns include medial
dislocation of the first metatarsal or lateral dislocation of some or all the lateral rays.
Type C injuries—Divergent incongruity of the midfoot joints in which the first metatarsal and
some or all of the lateral rays displace in opposite directions.
Midfoot injury classification systems are not especially helpful for stratifying prognosis or
management; however, an understanding of the injury is important in developing a treatment
plan
Most often, the second through fifth metatarsals move together as a unit. They may displace
laterally and/or dorsally.
The first metatarsal may move laterally with the others or may be divergent, displacing
independently. If divergent, the first metatarsal may displace along with the medial cuneiform
so that the plane of injury travels between the medial and middle cuneiform and then
between the medial cuneiform and the navicular.
In high-energy injuries, fractures or dislocations of the cuneiforms also may be present.
Figure 2 Illustrations of the foot and ankle show the Lisfranc classification of joint injuries.

Evaluation/Diagnosis
Patient History
In isolated injuries, the patient will present with foot pain.
In polytrauma patients, other injuries may be distracting. A thorough secondary and tertiary
examination of the patient will be important in detecting a foot injury.
Physical Examination
Midfoot swelling and tenderness will be present.
In subtle injuries, clues to the diagnosis include:
Midfoot pain with weight bearing
A positive piano key test, in which the first and second metatarsal heads are grasped and
moved relative to one another in the parasagittal plane. Pain at the midfoot suggests injury.
The forefoot pronation-abduction test also may be pathognomonic for tarsometatarsal
injury. In this test a dorsiflexion and eversion moment on the midfoot may elicit pain.
Ecchymosis on the plantar surface of the foot is very suspicious for midfoot injury.
Imaging Studies
Radiography
Radiographic evaluation
Internal oblique, AP, and lateral views of the foot
On an AP radiograph, alignment of the first and second rays is assessed.
The medial border of the first metatarsal should line up with the medial border of the medial
cuneiform.
The medial border of the second metatarsal should line up with the medial border of the
middle cuneiform.
Gapping (diastasis) of more than 2 mm between the medial cuneiform and the base of the
second metatarsal is considered substantial.
Rotation of the oblique radiograph will determine the rays that are visualized.
The third metatarsal should line up with the lateral cuneiform.

If the view is more oblique, the relationship of the fourth metatarsal to the cuboid is
observed.
A comparison radiograph of the uninjured foot may be helpful.
On a lateral radiograph, the dorsal cortex of the metatarsal bases should not be superior to
the dorsal cortex of the cuneiforms. Occasionally, this is subtle but is a sign of midfoot injury.
The fleck sign is a small avulsed fragment of bone in the interval between the bases of the first
and second metatarsal bones. This represents avulsion of metatarsal bone by the Lisfranc
ligament from its insertion at the base of the second metatarsal.
Weight-bearing or stress radiographs should be obtained if the results of physical examination
and plain radiographs are equivocal (Figure 3).

Computed Tomography
CT can be performed to better define injuries, especially in deciding whether an injury requires
surgical management.
In mild injuries, CT can determine if substantial displacement is present; reconstruction images
may be especially helpful.
Magnetic Resonance Imaging
MRI is not necessary for most midfoot injuries
Tears of the Lisfranc ligament observed on MRI in patients without displacement likely will not
benefit from surgical management.
MRI will reveal other injuries of questionable importance, including partial tears of the
peroneus longus at its insertion, and bruising or nondisplaced fractures of the bones of the
midfoot.
Management
Injuries with substantial displacement will benefit from surgical management. The challenge is
in defining how much displacement is substantial. Displacement observed on stress
radiographs may be more important than that observed on plain radiographs.
Diastasis of more than 3 or 4 mm between the medial cuneiform and the second metatarsal is
considered too severe for nonsurgical management. Diastasis of less than 2 mm usually is
acceptable for nonsurgical management.
If displacement is 2 to 3 mm, other factors may be essential in deciding the best treatment
option.
Stress or weight-bearing radiographs may demonstrate more displacement and support
surgical management.
Any dorsal displacement of the metatarsals relative to the cuneiforms should be managed
surgically.
Mild midfoot sprains without displacement can be managed with the use of a cast or a
removable cast boot, with patients using crutches and remaining non–weight bearing for less
than 6 weeks.

Patients are transitioned to a supportive shoe by 4 to 6 weeks, with progressive
rehabilitation.
A semiflexible foot orthosis with good arch support is helpful.
More severe midfoot injuries with 1 to 2 mm of Lisfranc ligament displacement may be
managed via as much as 6 weeks of non–weight bearing.
After the decision to proceed with surgical management is made, several options can be
selected:
Percutaneous reduction and fixation
Open reduction and internal fixation
Open reduction and primary fusion
Historically, the results of percutaneous reduction and Kirschner wire fixation of displaced
injuries have been disappointing and may lead to malreduction with posttraumatic arthritis
and deformity. This is related to the time required for the injury to heal because pins usually
are removed before 16 weeks postoperatively.
More recently, surgeons have used specially designed percutaneous clamps to reduce the
second metatarsal in patients with a mildly displaced injury. Fixation with the use of a screw
from the medial cuneiform to the second metatarsal may maintain reduction.
This technique may reduce slightly displaced injuries.
Given that the goal of surgical management is to anatomically reduce the midfoot, open
reduction has been the standard of care.
A longitudinal incision is made dorsally over the first interspace. Deeper dissection is
performed between the long and short extensors to the great toe, with the neurovascular
bundle protected with the extensor hallucis brevis laterally. A second incision is made
dorsally over the fourth metatarsal if access to the third or fourth metatarsals is necessary.
Direct reduction of the metatarsals is performed after removing any interposed tissues, and
reduction is provisionally maintained with the use of wires. Supination and adduction of the
forefoot often aids in reduction. Because the surfaces of the joints are flat, it may be tricky to
reduce the joints anatomically. Intraoperative imaging is important.
Definitive fixation can be achieved with the use of transarticular screws.
Solid screws are favored by some surgeons to decrease the risk of screw fracture after
weight bearing is initiated.
Dorsal bridging plates can be used to span areas of comminution or to reduce trauma to
the articular cartilage (Figure 4).
Compression across articular surfaces should be avoided.
The medial three rays are fixed rigidly, and the lateral two are fixed with the use of wires.

Mobility is more important for the lateral joints.
In many patients with mild to moderate injury, the fourth and fifth metatarsals reduce well
and do not require fixation.
Reduction with primary fusion of the medial three joints also is a treatment option, especially
in patients who primarily have a dislocation. The medial three joints are more important for
stability than mobility.
Surgeons have noted high rates of midfoot pain, enough to lead to midfoot fusion, in
patients treated via open reduction and internal fixation. Therefore, primary fusion has
been proposed.
In performing open reduction and fixation, the surgeon often will note that the joints can
be fixed a few millimeters up or down or sideways. These mild discrepancies are not visible
on plain radiographs; therefore, it is possible surgeons are rigidly fixing the joints slightly
off. Perhaps this is the reason many experienced surgeons tend to perform primary fusion.
A prospective randomized study found that patients with mostly ligamentous midfoot
injuries who underwent primary fusion had better outcomes.1 Another study found
outcomes were similar, with the only difference being the rate of hardware removal was
higher in the fixation group.2
Postoperative management depends on the treatment option performed and the specific
injury. Patients treated surgically should remain non–weight bearing for 6 to 8 weeks. In the
past, some surgeons would require 3 months of non–weight bearing and would remove
hardware before allowing weight bearing.
Currently, hardware is left in place much longer because patients may not be bothered by
the hardware and to decrease the risk for late displacement.

Complications
Late posttraumatic osteoarthritis is common in patients with a tarsometatarsal injury,
occurring in as many as 72% of patients. Anatomic reduction, open injury, smoking, and
comminution predict outcomes.
More than 2 mm of displacement or 15° of angulation are associated with a poorer prognosis.
Similar to most orthopaedic trauma, the outcomes of injuries in which the overall anatomy is
restored generally are better than injuries in which considerable deformity persists.
